question: A 7-year-old with a Gartland III supracondylar humerus fracture has a palpable radial pulse but cannot make the 'OK sign' (pinch index finger to thumb). Which structure is most likely injured?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension. The 'OK sign' tests the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), a motor branch of the median nerve.

answers.text: Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) — causing loss of FPL and FDP-index motor function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The AIN is the most commonly injured nerve in supracondylar fractures. It has no sensory territory, so presentation is purely motor: inability to flex the IP joint of thumb (FPL) and index finger (FDP) — tested by the 'OK sign'.

answers.text: Ulnar nerve — causing clawing of the ring and little fingers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ulnar nerve injury is less common in supracondylar fractures; it causes clawing of ring and little fingers with loss of intrinsics, not the 'OK sign' failure.

answers.text: Brachial artery — the absent pulse confirms complete arterial transection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pulse is palpable here, making complete arterial transection unlikely. AIN injury is a neurological finding distinct from vascular status.

overallFeedback.feedback: The AIN (anterior interosseous nerve) is the most commonly injured nerve in supracondylar fractures. Test it specifically with the 'OK sign'; it has no sensory component.
Correct. AIN = motor only (no sensation) = 'OK sign' test. Always test AIN in supracondylar fractures even if the pulse is present.
